justice: Both sides of the street appear to have sidewalks (right-side paved sidewalk and a left-side sidewalk behind the green construction fence), indicating some baseline spatial provision for pedestrians rather than car-only design.

The left side is heavily constrained by temporary roadworks (yellow metal barriers and multiple traffic cones), reducing equitable access to continuous pedestrian space on that side compared with the right side.

Accessibility is moderate because the right sidewalk looks continuous and relatively clear, but curb transitions/ramps are not visible at this segment, and the work-zone edge conditions may create barriers for some users (e.g., people pushing strollers or carts).
safety: Work-zone devices (yellow barriers and cones) provide clear visual channelization, which can reduce sudden conflicts between vehicles and the roadside work area.
The roadway is relatively narrow with no median separation and limited lane markings visible, which can increase risk of close passing and ambiguous positioning for drivers and cyclists.
Sidewalk protection from moving traffic is weak on the right side (no bollards/guardrail between curb and roadway), so pedestrians are mainly protected only by the curb.
livability: Street frontage is dominated by fences/walls (green construction hoarding on the left and a long wall/fence on the right), creating a low-activity edge with few visible destinations at ground level.
Very limited visible street furniture (no benches, small public spaces, or gathering points) reduces opportunities to linger and socialize for all users.
Low pedestrian presence and limited storefront activity in view suggest a corridor that functions more as a through-route than a vibrant neighborhood street.
sustainability: Mature trees and greenery are present along the corridor (notably on the left and right mid-ground), supporting urban ecosystem services and some carbon/heat mitigation.
Car travel is accommodated with a clear carriageway and active vehicle movement, but there is no visible public-transit stop infrastructure in the frame, limiting support for mode shift.
The absence of visible cycling facilities (no marked bike lanes, no protected space, no bike parking) reduces sustainable mobility options.
aesthetics: Green tree canopies along the street add visual softness and natural interest, improving the streetscape compared with a fully hardscaped corridor.
Construction hoarding, temporary barriers, and cones create visual clutter and a utilitarian appearance, lowering overall streetscape quality.
Building facades on the right are repetitive and somewhat worn/industrial in character (fencing and long blank edges), resulting in modest visual appeal.
comfort: Thermal comfort is moderate: trees provide some shade potential, but the roadway and sidewalks are largely exposed and the sky is bright, suggesting limited continuous shading along the walking path.
Physical comfort for walking is mixed: the right sidewalk surface appears relatively even, but the corridor lacks benches/rest points and has long monotonous edges (walls/fences).
Psychological comfort is reduced by the work-zone presence (barriers/cones) and limited 'eyes on the street' due to few active frontages and low pedestrian activity.
walkability: A continuous right-side sidewalk is visible and appears passable without major obstructions in this segment, supporting basic pedestrian movement.

Walkability is weakened by limited crossings or pedestrian priority features visible (no marked crosswalks or curb extensions in frame), which can make route continuity across the street harder when needed.
The left-side pedestrian realm is compromised by construction management (hoarding and channelization), reducing overall network continuity for pedestrians on both sides.
bikeability: No dedicated cycling infrastructure is visible (no bike lane markings, no physical protection, no shared-lane signage), making cycling depend on mixing with motor traffic.
The narrow carriageway and unclear lane definition increase potential close-pass and overtaking conflicts for cyclists.
Work-zone narrowing and channelization (cones/barriers) can force cyclists into less predictable positions, increasing interaction risk with vehicles.
